explanations.explanation: That's it. God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech, who reigned over Israel, and the leaders of Shechem. Animosity is bad blood, the kind of ill will that sours a relationship. It also caused them to treat Abimelech deceitfully (Judges 9:23).

Fear is a fair guess, since plenty of people in this story have reason to be nervous. But the text says God sent “…a spirit of animosity…” between Abimelech, who reigned over Israel, and the leaders of Shechem (Judges 9:23). That's ill will, not fright. It shows up as the leaders treating Abimelech deceitfully.

A spirit of wisdom would have been a lovely gift, friend, but that's not what the text says. God sent “…a spirit of animosity…” (Judges 9:23), which means bad blood. It lands between Abimelech, who reigned over Israel, and the leaders of Shechem. And it causes them to treat him deceitfully.

explanations.answer: So justice comes for the seventy sons
explanations.explanation: Right, and the text says it outright. It was “…in order that the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come to justice…” (Judges 9:24). Jerubbaal is the man also called Gideon (Judges 6:32). Their blood is to be avenged on Abimelech and on the Shechem leaders who helped him.

explanations.answer: So Israel turns back to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a happy ending, but this verse doesn't say it. The text gives a different reason: the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal was to come to justice (Judges 9:24). Jerubbaal, also called Gideon (Judges 6:32), was their father. I'd keep my eyes on the seventy here.

explanations.answer: So Midian stays out of the land
explanations.explanation: Midian doesn't come up anywhere in this passage, friend. The reason the text gives is that “…the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal…” might “…come to justice…” (Judges 9:24). Their blood is to be avenged on Abimelech and on the Shechem leaders who helped him murder his brothers. The whole thing turns on those seventy sons.

Not quite, friend. The text says their blood would be avenged “…on their brother Abimelech and on the leaders of Shechem, who had helped him murder his brothers.” (Judges 9:24). So Abimelech doesn't answer alone. The leaders who helped him are in it with him.

Correct. Abimelech is not the only one. The text says the blood of the seventy sons would be avenged “…on their brother Abimelech and on the leaders of Shechem, who had helped him murder his brothers.” (Judges 9:24). Both are named, and both are going to answer for it.

Yes. The Shechem leaders ambush from the hilltops and rob everyone passing by, and this is reported to Abimelech. Now the king knows something is up. The report goes straight to the man the ambush was set against.

explanations.answer: It reaches the elders of Israel
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text names one person. It says this was reported to Abimelech. Nothing in the verse mentions elders. The report goes to the man the ambush was set against.
The Philistines never show up in this passage, friend. The text says this was reported to Abimelech, the man the ambush was set against. That's where the news lands.

They cursed him, and they did it as they ate and drank in the house of their god. Imagine a festival where the entertainment is cursing the king. Gaal son of Ebed, the newcomer the leaders put their confidence in, is about to speak up too (Judges 9:26, 28). The mood in that room is not friendly to Abimelech.

Praise would have made Abimelech's week, but that's not what the text says. As they ate and drank in the house of their god, they cursed him. This is the same city whose leaders made him king (Judges 9:6). Now the talk at the festival is cursing.

Close, because the leaders of Shechem did make him king back at Judges 9:6. But at this festival the text says they cursed him as they ate and drank. Nobody is making him anything now, friend. They're cursing him.

That's what he says. Gaal son of Ebed, a newcomer the Shechem leaders have put their confidence in, claims that if the people were under his authority, he would remove Abimelech. He adds a dare: “Muster your army and come out!” That's a lot of nerve for a man who just arrived.

Peace would have been quieter, friend, but Gaal son of Ebed isn't in that mood. He says that if the people were under his authority, he would remove Abimelech. He even dares him: “Muster your army and come out!” (Judges 9:29). That's not an olive branch.

Gaal son of Ebed is going the other way. Earlier he asks, “Why should we serve Abimelech?” (Judges 9:28). Then he says that if the people were under his authority, he would remove Abimelech. Serving him is the last thing on his mind.

True. Zebul, the governor of the city, burned with anger when he heard Gaal, and he covertly sent messengers to Abimelech. The message says Gaal and his brothers have come to Shechem and are stirring up the city against him. Zebul heard it all and didn't sit on it.

This one is true, friend. Zebul, the governor of the city, heard Gaal's words and burned with anger. Then he covertly sent messengers to Abimelech to say that Gaal and his brothers were stirring up the city against him (Judges 9:31). Zebul is quietly on Abimelech's side.

explanations.answer: Lie in wait tonight and attack at sunrise
explanations.explanation: Yes. Zebul tells Abimelech and his people to come tonight and lie in wait in the fields. Then at sunrise they are to advance against the city. When Gaal and his men come out, Abimelech is to do to them whatever he is able. Zebul sent that message covertly, so I bet he did not want it to be read out loud at the gate!

explanations.answer: March in at noon with trumpets blowing
explanations.explanation: A loud noon parade would warn everybody, friend. Zebul's plan is the opposite. Abimelech and his people are to come tonight and lie in wait in the fields. Then they advance against the city at sunrise.

explanations.answer: Stay away until Gaal leaves the city
explanations.explanation: Zebul doesn't tell him to stay away until Gaal leaves. He does say to wait, but in the fields: come tonight and lie in wait there. Then in the morning at sunrise, they advance against the city. The waiting leads to an attack, friend, not to staying away.

explanations.answer: The shadows of the mountains look like men to you
explanations.explanation: That's his answer. Gaal sees people coming down from the mountains, and Zebul, the governor of the city, tells him the shadows of the mountains look like men to him. He brushes off what Gaal is pointing at. Then Gaal says it again and points to people coming from the center of the land (Judges 9:36-37).

explanations.answer: Those are only shepherds bringing in their flocks
explanations.explanation: Shepherds would be a calm answer, but the text has something sharper. Zebul says, “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you.” He's brushing off what Gaal sees. No flocks come up at all.

explanations.answer: Those are travelers coming up for the festival
explanations.explanation: The festival was already over, friend. They'd gone into the house of their god and cursed Abimelech at it. When Gaal points at the people coming down from the mountains, Zebul says, “The shadows of the mountains look like men to you.” He doesn't mention travelers at all.

Fight is right. Zebul asks, “Where is your gloating now?” and reminds Gaal what he said about Abimelech. Then he tells him to go out now and fight them. Zebul takes Gaal's own words and hands them right back.

Joining sounds friendly, but Zebul isn't being friendly. He asks, “Where is your gloating now?” and points out that these are the people Gaal ridiculed. Then he tells him to go out now and fight them. Gaal talked big, and Zebul is calling him on it.

Nobody is getting a welcome here, friend. Zebul asks Gaal, “Where is your gloating now?” and reminds him he ridiculed these very people. Then he says, “Go out now and fight them!” That's a dare, not a greeting.

explanations.answer: Gaal flees and many Shechemites fall wounded
explanations.explanation: That's how it goes. Gaal went out and fought, but Abimelech pursued him and Gaal fled. Many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. Gaal said he'd remove Abimelech, and it was Gaal who ran.

explanations.answer: Abimelech flees back to the mountains
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around. Abimelech pursued Gaal, and Gaal was the one who fled. Many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. Abimelech was the one doing the chasing.

explanations.answer: Both sides make peace at the gate
explanations.explanation: No peace talks at that gate, friend. Gaal fought Abimelech, then Abimelech pursued him and Gaal fled. Many Shechemites fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate. It's a hard moment for the city.

explanations.answer: Lies in wait and attacks them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Abimelech hears the people have gone into the fields, so he takes his men and lies in wait. When he sees the people coming out of the city, he rises up against them and attacks. Once again he sets up an ambush.

explanations.answer: Sends them a message of peace
explanations.explanation: No olive branch from this king. When Abimelech hears the people have come out into the fields, he takes his men and lies in wait. Then he rises up against them and attacks. Peace is not what he's carrying.

The text never sends him home. When the report reaches him, Abimelech takes his men, divides them and lies in wait in the fields. Then he rises up and attacks the people coming out of the city. He's staying right where the action is.
True. He takes his men and divides them into three companies. Last time, he set out by night and lay in wait against Shechem in four (Judges 9:34). So he's mixing it up this time.

This one is true, friend. Abimelech divides his men into three companies. The earlier attack used four (Judges 9:34), so this time the count is different. Abimelech and the companies with him take their stand at the entrance of the city gate, and the other two companies go against everyone in the fields.

Demolished is right. After a full day of fighting, Abimelech captured the city and killed its people. Then he demolished it and sowed it with salt. It's a hard thing to read, and I think it's fine to feel that.
Rebuilding is the opposite of what happens. Abimelech captures the city, kills its people, then demolishes it. After that he sows it with salt. Nothing about this ends with new walls.
No new walls went up, friend. Abimelech captured the city and killed its people. Then he demolished it and sowed it with salt. Fortifying is the reverse of what he does.

A branch, exactly. Abimelech takes his axe, cuts a branch from the trees and lifts it to his shoulder. Then he tells his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” This one is heavy, friend, because the branches are about to be used against the people in the inner chamber.

There's no house in this scene, friend. At Mount Zalmon, Abimelech takes his axe and cuts a branch from the trees. He lifts it to his shoulder and tells his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” The wood comes right off the trees.

A banner would be a showy way to march, but it's not in the text. Abimelech takes his axe and cuts a branch from the trees. He lifts it to his shoulder, and then each of his men cuts his own branch and follows him. It's a plain branch.
Not this time, friend. With the branch on his shoulder, Abimelech says to his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” So he's not sending them back. He wants them right there copying him.
False, and the text is clear. Abimelech tells his men, “Hurry and do what you have seen me do.” Then each man cuts his own branch and follows him. Nobody stays behind.

explanations.answer: About a thousand men and women
explanations.explanation: That's the number the text gives: about a thousand men and women. The branches were piled against the inner chamber and set on fire above them. It kills everyone in the tower of Shechem. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.

Seventy is a number from this story, but it belongs to Abimelech's brothers (Judges 9:24). The text says about a thousand men and women died in the tower of Shechem. It's a heavy part of the story. I think it's worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: About four hundred men and women
explanations.explanation: The text gives a bigger number than that. It says about a thousand men and women died when the chamber was set on fire above them. Everyone in the tower of Shechem was killed. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.
True. When Abimelech comes to attack the tower in Thebez, he approaches its entrance to set it on fire. He's right up at the door. That's close, and it matters in the next verse.
This one is true, friend. The text says Abimelech approached the entrance of the tower to set it on fire. He didn't stay back at a distance. He was right up against it.

An upper millstone is right. A woman dropped it on Abimelech's head, and it crushed his skull. That's the top stone of a grinding set. It came down from the roof where the people of Thebez had gone up.

A clay jar is a good guess, but the text names something else. A woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head, crushing his skull. That's the top stone used for grinding. It came from the roof of the tower.
There's no tent peg in this scene, friend. The text says a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head. It crushed his skull. That's the one object the verse gives.

explanations.answer: Draw his sword and kill him
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Abimelech quickly calls his armor-bearer and tells him, “Draw your sword and kill me…” The armor-bearer runs his sword through him, and he dies. It's a hard scene, and the text doesn't soften it.

The text doesn't send him anywhere. Abimelech quickly calls his armor-bearer and says, “Draw your sword and kill me…” The armor-bearer then runs his sword through him, and he dies. That's the end of Abimelech's story.

explanations.answer: Go and bring Zebul to him
explanations.explanation: Zebul isn't called for here, friend. Abimelech quickly calls his armor-bearer and says, “Draw your sword and kill me…” Then the armor-bearer runs his sword through him. Abimelech dies right there.

Woman is right. Abimelech says, “…lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’…” That's the reason he gives for what he asks. It tells us what was on his mind in his last moments, and it's his own reason, not God's.
A servant isn't in the line, friend. Abimelech says, “…lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’…” That's the reason he gives. It was a woman who dropped the millstone on his head.
No child is mentioned here. Abimelech says, “…lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’…” That's his stated reason for calling his armor-bearer. A woman is the one who dropped the millstone.
That's it. When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home. No crowning of a new king, no rebuilding, just heading home. The story of his rule closes quietly.
Gaal isn't back in this story. Earlier Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem (Judges 9:41). When the Israelites see Abimelech is dead, they all go home. Nobody is crowned.
Nobody picks up a hammer, friend. Abimelech had demolished the city and sowed it with salt. When the Israelites see he's dead, the text says they all go home. That's all they do.

Yes, Jotham, Jerubbaal's son. The text says God brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them. That wraps up the story of Abimelech and Shechem.

Gaal had plenty to say, but the curse isn't his. The text says God brought the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them. Gaal is the newcomer who talked big and then fled.

Zebul, the governor of the city, has a big part in the story, but the curse isn't his. The text says the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon the men of Shechem. God brought their wickedness back upon their own heads. Jotham is the name to remember.
